title: Where Love Is, God Is
text:
Martin Avdeitch was a shoemaker who lived in a basement room with one window onto the street. Through it he saw people's feet, and he knew many of them by their boots. His wife and children had all died, the last a little son, and Martin had fallen into despair until an old pilgrim told him to live for God. He began to read the Gospels every evening, and his heart grew lighter.

One night he dozed over the book and heard a voice: "Martin, look out into the street tomorrow, for I shall come."

The next day he kept looking out of the window. He saw old Stepanitch, a retired soldier, shoveling snow and shivering, and called him in for hot tea. Later he saw a young mother in thin summer clothes trying to shelter her baby from the cold. He brought her in, fed her, and gave her his old cloak and a little money. In the afternoon an old woman caught a boy stealing an apple from her basket and seized him by the hair. Martin went out, made peace between them, and paid for the apple, and the boy ended up helping the old woman carry her sack.

That evening Martin sat sadly with his Gospel, since the visitor had not come. Then he heard the voice ask whether he did not know him, and saw the soldier, the mother with her baby, and the old woman with the boy, each smiling. The book lay open at the words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
lesson: The chances to do real good usually come through the ordinary people who pass your window each day. Pay attention to them.
people: Martin Avdeitch the cobbler, Stepanitch, a young mother, an apple seller and a boy
source: Leo Tolstoy, Where Love Is, God Is (1885)
